planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in a gritty, humus-rich, well-drained woodland or rock-garden soil in partial to full shade, setting the small rhizome about 1-2 inches deep; snow trillium is one of the very earliest spring ephemerals and needs sharp drainage rather than the constantly wet soil favored by larger trilliums.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, only 1-2 inches deep, in a spot that stays cool and does not become waterlogged over winter. Trillium nivale is the smallest and among the earliest-blooming of the North American trilliums, often pushing its tiny white flowers up through late snow cover weeks before most other woodland wildflowers appear. Its diminutive scale suits a shaded rock garden, trough, or the front edge of a woodland path where such an early bloomer would otherwise be overlooked. Purchase only nursery-propagated stock, since wild populations are uncommon and slow to recover from collection.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting the rhizome 2-3 inches deep; relict trillium is a federally protected mottled-leaf species found only in scattered river-bluff woodlands of the Deep South and should be sourced only from nursery propagation.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, 2-3 inches deep, on a gentle slope similar to the river-bluff hardwood forests where it naturally grows. Trillium reliquum is a sessile-flowered, mottled-leaf trillium native to a small area spanning Georgia, Alabama, and South Carolina, bearing a maroon to yellow-green stalkless flower nestled directly atop richly patterned foliage. It is federally listed as endangered in the wild, so it is a conservation-minded addition for a shaded native plant collection when obtained from a reputable propagating nursery rather than wild-collected. Give it a stable, undisturbed spot beneath deciduous canopy alongside other spring ephemerals.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting the rhizome 2-3 inches deep with the growing tip up; southern red trillium naturally occurs in rich cove-forest soils of the southern Appalachians and rewards deep, fertile plantings.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in deep, moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, 2-3 inches deep, replicating the rich cove-forest floor of its native Appalachian range. Trillium sulcatum produces one of the largest flowers of any eastern trillium, a stalked, deep maroon-red bloom with distinctly furrowed (sulcate) sepals held above broad, richly veined leaves in mid-spring. Its bold flower size and clump-forming habit make it a striking specimen for a shaded woodland border, best appreciated near a path where the large blossoms can be seen up close. It combines well with ferns, foamflower, and other spring ephemerals under high deciduous canopy.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; unlike many Arisaema species, this one tolerates drier soil and more sun once its foliage has expanded, making it useful in a woodland edge planting.

directions: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in a partly shaded woodland-edge bed; give it drier conditions in summer dormancy than most cobra lilies require. Arisaema flavum has an extraordinarily wide native range across the Himalayas, the Middle East, and East Africa, and stands out among jack-in-the-pulpits for its small, bright egg-yolk-yellow spathe rather than the typical green or purple-striped hood. Its compact size and unusual sunny color make it a distinctive accent for a partly shaded rock garden or the front of a woodland bed, where it multiplies gradually by offsets over time.

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; this is among the hardiest and most cold-tolerant Arisaema species, native to cool temperate forests of northeastern Asia.

directions: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Arisaema amurense is native to the cold forests of Manchuria, Korea, and the Russian Far East, giving it exceptional winter hardiness compared with many other jack-in-the-pulpit species, and it produces a green-and-white-striped spathe above deeply divided, five- to seven-part leaflets in mid-spring, followed by a spike of bright red berries in fall. Its cold tolerance makes it a good choice for northern woodland gardens where more tender Arisaema species struggle, and the fall berry display extends its season of interest well past bloom time.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; this mayapple relative is grown chiefly for its large, glossy, deeply lobed umbrella-like foliage that emerges bronze before turning deep green.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving each clump ample room for its large leaves to spread. Podophyllum versipelle is a Chinese woodland species prized for its bold, glossy, deeply cut leaves held on tall petioles like a cluster of umbrellas, with small maroon flowers hidden beneath the foliage in spring followed by orange-red fruit in fall. Its dramatic, oversized leaf form makes it an excellent architectural foliage plant for the back of a shaded border or a shaded courtyard bed where its scale can be appreciated against finer-textured companions like ferns or epimediums.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Warley barrenwort is a vigorous hybrid grown for its coppery-orange spring flowers set against semi-evergreen, spiny-edged foliage.

directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, then cut back old foliage in late winter before new flower spikes emerge. Epimedium x warleyense is a robust hybrid named for the historic Warley Place garden in England, valued for its unusual coppery-orange, yellow-centered flowers that appear in loose sprays above bronze-tinted new foliage in spring. It is more vigorous and sun-tolerant than many epimedium species, spreading steadily by rhizome to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover under trees and shrubs. Its warm flower color pairs well with the more common yellow and white epimediums for extended seasonal contrast in a shaded border.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Farges' barrenwort forms a slowly spreading clump with red-mottled new growth and delicate pink to white spring flowers.

directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where the plant can build a slowly expanding clump over several seasons. Epimedium fargesii is a west-central Chinese species with narrow, spiny-margined leaflets that emerge mottled with red-bronze tones before maturing to green, complemented by loose sprays of small pink-to-white, long-spurred flowers in spring. Its refined foliage texture and subtle flower color suit a shaded woodland or rock garden setting where it can be viewed up close, and it combines well with hellebores and hardy ferns as a long-lived, low-maintenance groundcover.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil at a pond or stream margin in partial shade in spring; giant Himalayan cowslip needs permanently damp soil and will not tolerate summer drought.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently wet, humus-rich soil at the margin of a stream, pond, or bog garden in partial shade in spring. Primula florindae is the largest of the commonly grown primroses, native to boggy meadows of the Tibetan plateau, sending up tall stems topped with a drooping, fragrant cluster of bell-shaped, sulfur-yellow flowers dusted with a pale mealy coating in mid to late summer, later than most other primroses bloom. Its late bloom time and tall stature make it a valuable addition to a shaded bog garden or water feature, extending the primrose season and pairing well with astilbe, rodgersia, and Japanese primrose along a damp woodland edge.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; orchid primrose is short-lived but produces a uniquely shaped bicolor flower spike unlike any other primrose.

directions: Plant divisions or nursery-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring, keeping the soil evenly damp through the growing season. Primula vialii is unmistakable among primroses for its dense, conical flower spike that opens from the bottom up, starting bright red-violet in bud and opening to lavender-blue flowers, creating a striking two-toned, poker-like bloom reminiscent of an orchid or a small red-hot-poker plant. Though often short-lived, it self-sows readily in congenial conditions to maintain a presence in the garden, making it a novel accent for a moist, partly shaded border or streamside planting where its unusual flower form stands out.

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil at a stream or pond margin in partial shade in spring; Sikkim cowslip is closely related to Primula florindae and shares its need for permanently damp soil.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently wet, humus-rich soil at a stream, pond, or bog margin in partial shade in spring. Primula sikkimensis is native to alpine meadows and stream banks of the eastern Himalayas, producing an upright stem topped with a nodding cluster of fragrant, pale yellow, bell-shaped flowers coated with a fine white mealy powder in early summer, blooming somewhat earlier than its close relative the giant Himalayan cowslip. Its fragrant, softly colored flowers and preference for reliably damp ground make it a good companion for candelabra primroses and moisture-loving ferns in a shaded bog garden or the damp margin of a woodland pond.
